title: 1. Environment setup
text: Set up the R environment used in the tutorial, either via the workshop cloud environment or locally on your laptop.

title: 1. Environment setup
text:
Option A (recommended): Workshop RStudio environment
A virtual machine running RStudio Server was available in PDC Cloud during the workshop.
This VM was only available during the workshop and is no longer accessible — use Option B below instead.
Resources were shared, so avoid creating additional large objects. The VM shut down after the workshop — save your work as an R script and download it via the Files pane (More → Export) before you leave.

Check required packages
All required packages are pre-installed in the workshop environment. Load them and confirm that they are available:
library(asvoccur)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)


Check access to example data
For this tutorial, ASV portal data is pre-downloaded and available on the virtual machine. Check access:
data_path <- "/srv/course-data/"
list.files(data_path)
If two (IBA_COI) zip files are listed, you are ready to proceed.

Option B (fallback): Run RStudio locally on your laptop
You will need to install:

R
RStudio
the following R packages:

remotes
asvoccur
vegan
ape
rworldmap

To install and load the required R packages:
# Install from CRAN
install.packages(c(
  "remotes",
  "vegan",
  "ape",
  "rworldmap",
  "lubridate"
))

# Install from GitHub
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/asvoccur")

# Load
library(asvoccur)
library(vegan)
library(ape)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)

# Confirm version
packageVersion("asvoccur")  # Should say 1.2.0

Download example data from the ASV portal
In this option, example data is downloaded directly from the ASV portal.

Go to the ASV portal start page.
Click DOWNLOAD. If you are not already logged in, you will be redirected to the login page.
If you do not already have an account, either:

sign in with a Google or GitHub account, or
create a new SBDI account.

On the Download page, under Download link, download both datasets used in this tutorial:

IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE
IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE

Place both zip files in a single folder, e.g.:
course-data/
├── IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE.zip
└── IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE.zip
Set the path to the data folder in R and confirm access:

data_path <- "local/path/to/course-data"
list.files(data_path)
If the expected zip file(s) are listed, you are ready to proceed.

title: 5. Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity)
text:
Examine diversity within each sample — alpha diversity — using the Shannon index, complementing the between-sample comparison of community composition in step 4.

Calculate Shannon diversity per sample
We reuse counts_filt, the cluster-aggregated matrix from step 4:
shannon <- vegan::diversity(counts_filt, MARGIN = 2)
A higher Shannon index indicates greater within-sample diversity, reflecting both the number of clusters present and how evenly their abundances are distributed.


Plot Shannon diversity by habitat
par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1))
boxplot(shannon ~ habitat[ix], las = 2, xlab = "",
        ylab = "Shannon diversity",
        col = habitat_cols[levels(factor(habitat[ix]))])
Shannon diversity is broadly similar across habitats, with overlapping distributions. This doesn’t contradict the PCoA in step 4: PCoA reflects which species are present, while Shannon reflects how many and how evenly distributed — habitats can differ in composition but have similar diversity levels.

title: Exploring eDNA in SBDI
text: Welcome to the Exploring eDNA in SBDI workshop at BioSyst EU 2026, Uppsala, 17–19 August 2026! This workshop demonstrates how eDNA/metabarcoding data can be accessed, processed and analysed within the Swedish Biodiversity Data Infrastructure (SBDI) — from data submission and processing through to exploring arthropod biodiversity patterns across Swedish habitat types, using COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas.

title: 4. Community differences (beta diversity)
text:
Analyse differences in community composition between samples — beta diversity — using Spearman correlation-based dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).

Aggregate ASVs to clusters
In addition to ASV taxonomy and BOLD BINs, the IBA data also include project-specific cluster assignments in the associatedSequences column. Here, we use these assignments to aggregate the ASVs into a smaller set of clusters.
The cluster assignments are read from loaded, because merge_data() drops the associatedSequences column when combining datasets.
cluster_lookup <- unique(data.table::rbindlist(lapply(loaded$asvs, function(x)
  x[, .(taxonID, associatedSequences)])))

cluster_id <- cluster_lookup$associatedSequences[
  match(rownames(merged$counts), cluster_lookup$taxonID)
]

# Check that every ASV maps to one cluster
stopifnot(
  sum(is.na(cluster_id)) == 0,
  anyDuplicated(cluster_lookup$taxonID) == 0
)

clevels <- unique(cluster_id)
cidx    <- match(cluster_id, clevels)

G <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(
  i = cidx,
  j = seq_along(cluster_id),
  x = 1,
  dims = c(length(clevels), length(cluster_id))
)

cluster_counts <- G %*% merged$counts
rownames(cluster_counts) <- clevels

nrow(cluster_counts)
This considerably reduces the size of the count table. We then subset the cluster-level table to the samples selected in step 3 and remove clusters that are absent from all of these samples. Such all-zero rows contain no information for comparing the selected samples.
counts_filt <- cluster_counts[, ix, drop = FALSE]
counts_filt <- counts_filt[Matrix::rowSums(counts_filt) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
counts_filt <- as.matrix(counts_filt)


Calculate a Spearman-based dissimilarity
Spearman correlation measures similarity in the rank order of cluster abundances between samples. We convert it to a 0–1 dissimilarity, where 0 indicates identical rankings and 1 opposite rankings:”
spear_cor  <- cor(counts_filt, method = "spearman")
spear_dist <- (1 - spear_cor) / 2


Run PCoA
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) represents the dissimilarities among samples in a smaller number of dimensions. We use a Cailliez correction because the Spearman-based dissimilarities are not necessarily Euclidean:
pcoa_res <- pcoa(spear_dist, correction = "cailliez")


Prepare colour scales
color_habitat and habitat_cols were already created in step 3. We add continuous colour scales for sampling date and latitude, plus colours for the two extraction methods:
ramp <- colorRampPalette(rev(c(
  "#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE090", "#FFFFBF", "#E0F3F8", "#91BFDB", "#4575B4"
)))

yday_range <- min(yday[ix], na.rm = TRUE):max(yday[ix], na.rm = TRUE)
color_yday <- ramp(length(yday_range))
yday_index <- yday - min(yday_range) + 1

lat_range <- floor(min(lat[ix], na.rm = TRUE)):ceiling(max(lat[ix], na.rm = TRUE))
color_lat <- ramp(length(lat_range))
lat_index <- round(lat) - min(lat_range) + 1

method      <- dataset_id[ix]
method_cols <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "#e76f51",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "#2a9d8f"
)
method_labs <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "homogenate",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "lysate"
)
For the legends, latitude is shown at 2-degree intervals and sampling date by month:
lat_ticks <- seq(ceiling(min(lat_range) / 2) * 2, max(lat_range), by = 2)

month_ticks  <- sort(tapply(yday[ix], month[ix], min))
month_labels <- month.abb[as.integer(names(month_ticks))]


Plot PCoA results
We plot the same PCoA four times, colouring samples by sampling date, habitat, latitude and extraction method:
xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[1] * 100), "%)")
ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(pcoa_res$values$Rel_corr_eig[2] * 100), "%)")

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 6), xpd = TRUE)

# Panel: colour by year-day
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_yday[yday_index[ix]], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by year-day")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = color_yday[month_ticks - min(yday_range) + 1],
       legend = month_labels)

# Panel: colour by habitat
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_habitat[ix], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by habitat")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = habitat_cols, legend = names(habitat_cols))

# Panel: colour by latitude
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = color_lat[lat_index[ix]], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by latitude")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = color_lat[lat_ticks - min(lat_range) + 1],
       legend = lat_ticks)

# Panel: colour by extraction method
plot(pcoa_res$vectors[, 1], pcoa_res$vectors[, 2],
     col = "black", bg = method_cols[as.character(method)], pch = 21, cex = 1,
     xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by extraction method")
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
       col = method_cols, legend = method_labs)
The first two PCoA axes each explain only about 4% of the variation, so the plots capture only part of the community differences. They suggest effects of habitat, sampling date and latitude, while homogenate and lysate samples are largely mixed.

title: 3. Sample mapping
text:
Explore the spatial distribution of samples and their associated habitat types across Sweden.

Inspect contextual data
Core sample-level metadata is available in merged_df$events:
colnames(merged_df$events)
Samples are ordered consistently across tables — rownames(merged_df$events), rownames(merged_df$emof) and colnames(merged$counts) all refer to the same samples:
identical(rownames(merged_df$events), rownames(merged_df$emof))



Extract spatial and temporal variables
Latitude and longitude can be used directly, whereas eventDate requires some preparation because dates in these two datasets are stored as start/end intervals. We therefore first extract the start of each interval before calculating month and day of year.
A few records only contain a year and no exact date. These cannot be assigned a month or day of year, so they are left as NA. We will exclude these records later when filtering the samples used in the analyses.
lat   <- as.numeric(merged_df$events$decimalLatitude)
lon   <- as.numeric(merged_df$events$decimalLongitude)

event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", merged_df$events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd")
)
month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)



Extract habitat type
The env_local_scale column contains habitat type classifications based on the Environment Ontology (ENVO). We first inspect the unique values:
unique(merged_df$events$env_local_scale)
For plotting, we create short labels and assign a colour to each habitat:
habitat_map <- c(
  "forested area [ENVO:00000111]"    = "forest",
  "area of cropland [ENVO:01000892]" = "cropland",
  "wetland area [ENVO:00000043]"     = "wetland",
  "grassland area [ENVO]"            = "grassland",
  "urban biome [ENVO:01000249]"      = "urban",
  "alpine biome [ENVO:01001835]"     = "alpine"
)
habitat <- habitat_map[merged_df$events$env_local_scale]

habitat_cols <- c(
  "forest"    = "#2d6a4f",
  "cropland"  = "#d4a017",
  "wetland"   = "#4895ef",
  "grassland" = "#95d5b2",
  "urban"     = "#adb5bd",
  "alpine"    = "#9b5de5"
)
color_habitat <- habitat_cols[habitat]



Filter samples and balance extraction methods
Samples with very few total reads are excluded, as their community composition is unreliable, and so are the handful with an incomplete eventDate (their yday is NA, see above):
sample_depth <- Matrix::colSums(merged$counts)
summary(sample_depth)  # inspect before picking a threshold
ix <- which(sample_depth >= 100000 & !is.na(yday))
length(ix)
100000 is a reasonable depth threshold here — check the summary() output above and adjust it if it excludes far more or fewer samples than expected for your dataset.
The two datasets differ in size (homogenate: ~860 samples; lysate: ~4,550). We balance them by keeping only samples from site+dates present in both:
dataset_id      <- factor(sub(":.*", "", colnames(merged$counts)))
event_date_only <- as.Date(event_start)
location_id     <- merged_df$events$locationID

hom_ix <- ix[dataset_id[ix] == "IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE"]
lys_ix <- ix[dataset_id[ix] == "IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE"]

# Keep only samples from site+dates present in both datasets
site_date_key <- function(ix) paste(location_id[ix], event_date_only[ix])
shared_keys <- intersect(unique(site_date_key(hom_ix)), unique(site_date_key(lys_ix)))

hom_paired <- hom_ix[site_date_key(hom_ix) %in% shared_keys]
lys_paired <- lys_ix[site_date_key(lys_ix) %in% shared_keys]
length(hom_paired) + length(lys_paired)
That’s 1,631 samples going into the PCoA in the next step — possibly heavier than our shared workshop VM can comfortably handle at once, so we downsample each method evenly down to a lighter total:
target_n <- 800
set.seed(1)
n_each <- target_n %/% 2
ix <- c(sample(hom_paired, size = min(n_each, length(hom_paired))),
        sample(lys_paired, size = min(n_each, length(lys_paired))))
length(ix)
From here on, ix is the fixed set of samples used throughout the rest of the tutorial — both extraction methods, pooled and paired.



Map samples
We define a function that plots monthly maps of the study area, showing where and when samples were collected, with point colour indicating habitat type:
plot_monthly_maps <- function() {
  newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")
  par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1), xpd = TRUE)

  for (m in 1:12) {
    ix_m <- ix[month[ix] == m]
    plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(55, 70), asp = 1, main = month.abb[m])
    if (length(ix_m) > 0) {
      points(lon[ix_m], lat[ix_m], pch = 21,
             col = "black", bg = color_habitat[ix_m], cex = 1.5)
    }
  }

  plot.new()
  legend("left", bty = "n", legend = names(habitat_cols),
         pt.bg = habitat_cols, pch = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
         title = "Habitat")
}

plot_monthly_maps()
This figure has several panels and can look cramped on a laptop screen — click Zoom above the Plots pane for a larger view. Points also overlap since paired samples share a location, and nearby sites (~10–15 km apart) can coincide at this scale — so it looks sparser than the actual sample count.

title: Import and analyse ASV portal data with R
text:
This tutorial walks through the main steps for importing and analysing ASV portal data in R. As a case study, we use COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas (IBA) project, which sampled arthropods at 200 sites across six habitat types in Sweden (forest, cropland, wetland, grassland, urban and alpine). We combine two Malaise-trap datasets generated using different extraction protocols — homogenate and lysate — to explore biodiversity patterns across habitats.

Environment setup — Access the workshop RStudio environment (or run locally)
Data preparation — Load, merge and aggregate data sourced from the ASV portal
Sample mapping — Filter, pair and map sampling coverage across Sweden and habitat types
Community differences (beta diversity) — Explore differences among samples using Spearman dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Examine Shannon diversity across habitat types
Taxonomic composition — Barplots across habitats and months

Get started →

Reference
Miraldo, A., Sundh, J., Iwaszkiewicz-Eggebrecht, E., Buczek, M., Goodsell, R., Johansson, H., Fisher, B. L., Raharinjanahary, D., Rajoelison, E. T., Ranaivo, C., Randrianandrasana, C., Rafanomezantsoa, J.-J., Manoharan, L., Granqvist, E., van Dijk, L. J. A., Alberg, L., Åhlén, D., Aspebo, M., Åström, S., … Ronquist, F. (2025). Data of the Insect Biome Atlas: A metabarcoding survey of the terrestrial arthropods of Sweden and Madagascar. Scientific Data, 12(1), 1–18.

text:
Example results from running the tutorial on two combined IBA COI datasets, IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE and IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE (paired by site and date, then downsampled and pooled), merged with merge_data().


Sampling sites across Sweden
One map per month of the paired, pooled IBA sampling sites, coloured by habitat type.




Community differences — beta diversity (PCoA)
Principal Coordinates Analysis (Spearman-based dissimilarity) of cluster-level community composition, coloured by year-day, habitat, latitude and extraction method. Homogenate and lysate samples are thoroughly mixed in the last panel — extraction method explains only ~0.2% of the variance in community composition (PERMANOVA), compared to ~7% for habitat — supporting pooling both for the rest of the analysis.




Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Shannon index
Diversity within each sample, by habitat — complementing the between-sample (beta diversity) view above.




Taxonomic composition by habitat
Mean monthly relative abundance of the most common insect orders in each of the six habitat types.

title: 2. Data preparation
text:
Load, merge and aggregate ASV portal data into a format suitable for downstream analyses.

Load the dataset(s)
Load the COI dataset(s) present in the data_path folder defined in the previous section:
loaded <- load_data(data_path)
This reads datasets into the loaded object, which you can inspect using the magnifying glass next to it in the Environment pane. The object is a list organised into data type sub-lists, each containing one table or matrix element per dataset:

counts: ASV read counts
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomic annotations
events: core sample-level metadata (where, when, how, who)
datasets: dataset-level metadata
emof: dataset-specific extended measurement or fact contextual data

Sparse matrices (dgCMatrix) are used to reduce memory usage for count data, while tabular structures (data.table) are used for metadata. To see dataset sizes, inspect the elements in counts, where sizes are shown as matrix dimensions (e.g. IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE: dgCMatrix [142153 x 862], corresponding to the number of ASVs × samples).
To see the full function documentation for load_data:
?asvoccur::load_data



Merge the dataset(s)
Next, we merge the datasets in order to analyse them jointly:
merged <- merge_data(loaded)
The merged object is a list with one combined object per data type (counts, events, asvs, datasets, emof), represented as a sparse matrix for count data and data tables for metadata, as in loaded.



Convert merged metadata to data frames
Convert the metadata tables to data frame format for convenience. merged$counts stays a sparse matrix — converting it to a dense data frame would be very memory-intensive for large datasets:
merged_df <- convert_to_df(merged)
In merged_df$counts, each row corresponds to an ASV and each column to a sample. To inspect the sample names:
colnames(merged$counts)
ASVs shared across datasets are merged using SBDI ASV IDs. These IDs correspond to MD5 hashes of the sequences, meaning that ASVs with identical sequences are represented only once.



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
We now aggregate ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels based on the taxonomic annotation:
cladecounts <- sum_by_clade(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
This produces aggregated counts at the following levels:

kingdom (or domain)
phylum
class
order
family
genus
species
otu (if available)

Both raw counts and normalised counts (relative abundances per sample) are available as sparse matrices. Dots represent zeros:
cladecounts$raw$phylum[1:3, 1:3]  # raw counts at phylum level
cladecounts$norm$order[8:10, 1:2]  # relative abundances at order level

title: 6. Taxonomic composition
text:
Summarise taxonomic composition across habitats and months using stacked barplots.

Define the barplot function
The function below identifies the most abundant taxa across the selected samples, calculates their mean relative abundance for each habitat and month, and displays the results as stacked barplots.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, size_taxa = -1, top_x = 10) {
  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))

  habitats <- names(habitat_cols)
  n_hab <- length(habitats)

  # ok is the same set of taxa in every panel, so we use one shared legend
  # in its own column, spanning the full figure height for readability
  layout(matrix(c(seq_len(n_hab), rep(n_hab + 1, n_hab)), nrow = n_hab),
         widths = c(4, 1.3))
  par(mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1))

  # Select the most abundant taxa across the samples retained in step 3
  ok <- sort(
    Matrix::rowMeans(cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix]),
    index.return = TRUE,
    decreasing = TRUE
  )$ix[1:top_x]

  if (size_taxa == -1) {
    size_taxa <- 2
  }

  for (hab in habitats) {
    ix_hab <- intersect(ix, which(habitat == hab))

    monthly_averages_matr <- matrix(
      ncol = 12,
      nrow = nrow(cladecounts$norm[[rank]])
    )

    for (j in 1:12) {
      ix2 <- intersect(ix_hab, which(month == j))

      if (length(ix2) > 1) {
        monthly_averages_matr[, j] <-
          Matrix::rowMeans(cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix2])
      }

      if (length(ix2) == 1) {
        monthly_averages_matr[, j] <-
          cladecounts$norm[[rank]][, ix2]
      }

      if (length(ix2) == 0) {
        monthly_averages_matr[, j] <- NA
      }
    }

    barplot(
      monthly_averages_matr[ok, ],
      col = mycols(length(ok)),
      main = hab
    )
  }

  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
  legend(
    "center",
    bty = "n",
    pch = 19,
    col = mycols(length(ok))[length(ok):1],
    cex = size_taxa,
    legend = rownames(cladecounts$norm[[rank]])[rev(ok)]
  )
}
The same paired sample set selected in step 3, stored in ix, is used both to select the most abundant taxa and to calculate the habitat-by-month averages.


Choose a taxonomic rank
sum_by_clade() stores abundance tables at several taxonomic ranks. The numeric rank codes are:

kingdom (or domain)
phylum
class
order
family
genus
species



Example: plot top orders
Plot the eight most abundant orders across habitats and months:
plot_barplots(rank = 4, top_x = 8)
